articles.title: When will you get your Social Security and Supplemental Security Income payments for November?
articles.summary: The exact date you can expect to receive your Social Security payment for the month varies from recipient to recipient. Here's who is eligible to receive pay...
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Social Security recipients typically receive their payments on the second, third, and fourth Wednesdays of the month.

The final round of October payments is going out on Oct. 28. However, there are a few exceptions when payments administered by the Social Security Administration fall on different dates.

For example, those who also receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), which is typically paid out on the first of each month, will receive their November payment on Friday of this week because Nov. 1 falls on a Sunday.

Here's what to know about this month's payments.

To be eligible for Social Security retirement benefits, you must be at least 62 years old and have earned at least 40 work credits — this is equal to about 10 years of work while paying Social Security taxes.

Beyond retirement, you may be eligible for Social Security benefits if you are disabled or blind and meet specific medical and work-credit criteria. Family members such as spouses, ex-spouses, survivors, dependent parents, and children of eligible workers may also qualify for payments. In that case, your payment would be based on the primary beneficiary's birthday.

Who is eligible for Supplemental Security Income benefits?

Supplemental Security Income, which is also administered by the Social Security Administration, provides monthly payments to people with disabilities and older adults who have little or no income or resources.

In some cases, retirees may qualify for Social Security benefits based on their work history, as well as SSI benefits due to their financial need.

Those who qualify for SSI include adults and children who have:

A disability, blindness, or are age 65 or older.

According to the Social Security Administration (SSA), payments are distributed based on the recipient's birth date. Typically, they arrive on the second, third, and fourth Wednesdays of each month.

Exactly which Wednesday will depend on your birth date.

Recipients who are born from the first to the 10th of the month receive their benefit on the second Wednesday of the month. If your birth date falls on the 11th to the 20th of the month, you'll receive your payment on the third Wednesday of the month. Those who are born on the 21st to the 31st of the month will receive their payment on the fourth Wednesday of the month.

Supplemental Security Income benefits are usually paid on the first of the month. If the first falls on a weekend or holiday, the payment is made on the preceding business day.

A full schedule of this year's Social Security payments is available on the Social Security Administration's website.

If your friend has received her Social Security check this month, but you haven't, there's no need to panic.

Payments are sent out in bundles based on birthdays, and for most people, they're electronically deposited directly into a federally insured bank account.

By law, all federal benefit payments — including Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits — must be made electronically with few exceptions. Your monthly benefit is either sent to your bank account via direct deposit or loaded onto a Direct Express Debit Mastercard. If you're applying for Social Security or Supplemental Security Income benefits, you can elect to receive your benefit payment in one of these methods electronically when you enroll .

If you currently receive Social Security or Supplemental Security Income benefits by check, you are in the minority and may need to switch to an electronic payment option if possible.

Direct deposits typically appear by 9 a.m. on your payment day. If your payment is late, check with your bank or financial institution to see if there has been a posting delay.

If you receive your benefits by paper check, it can take up to three business days to receive your benefits. If that doesn't happen, contact the SSA via phone at 800-772-1213, or online through your My Social Security account.

Your My Social Security account is a free personalized portal where you can request a replacement Social Security card, check the status of a benefits application, estimate future benefits, or manage the benefits you already receive. You can set up an account even if you don't currently receive benefits.

Confirm that the SSA has your correct bank information and address, and it's a good idea to sign up for SSA to notify you when the payment is sent out.

You can apply to start your Social Security checks via your My Social Security account or make an appointment with an agent in person or by phone at 800-333-1795. You select the month you want your benefit to start in your application. After you apply, SSA will send you a letter confirming that your benefits are approved or that you need to provide more information.

It typically takes at least a month to receive your first Social Security check after your application is processed. The precise timing of your payment delivery relies on processing times at the Social Security Administration. Right now, staffing cuts and other backend tech disruptions are raising alarms.

During an SSA operations meeting in April , an official from the agency reported that the field offices "are struggling right now to keep pace with the timeliness this year."

That's why it's smart to apply up to four months before you want to start receiving benefits.

As Jason Fichtner, executive director of the Retirement Income Institute who served in several positions at the Social Security Administration, warned in an interview: "With SSA staff being reduced while the agency was already operating at insufficient support levels and computer systems in need of modernization, continued service delays, and breakdowns are likely."

The Social Security COLA will increase by 3.6% in 2027, according to the Social Security Administration.

articles.title: First time health buyers increased 3.8X since FY22: Policybazaar
articles.summary: MUMBAI: First-time health insurance buyers on Policybazaar increased 277% to nearly 18 lakhs between FY22 and FY26, with smaller cities accounting for 67%
articles.body: MUMBAI: First-time health insurance buyers on Policybazaar increased 277% to nearly 18 lakhs between FY22 and FY26, with smaller cities accounting for 67% of new customers, according to data shared by the online insurance platform. The trend points to wider adoption beyond metropolitan centres, with buyers also opting for higher coverage.The number of first-time buyers grew 5% in FY23, 40% in FY24, 67% in FY25 and 54% in FY26. The data comes amid IRDAI's focus on expanding insurance coverage to the “missing middle”, or people who remain outside the insurance system.First-time buyers from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities grew 351% between FY22 and FY26, outpacing overall growth in each of the four years. Their share of new buyers rose to 67% in FY26 from 56% in FY22. Around seven in 10 additional first-time buyers during this period came from these cities.Cities in Kerala recorded some of the highest growth rates. Malappuram grew 128.34% year on year, followed by Kottayam at 122.66%, Alappuzha at 120.76%, Thiruvananthapuram at 114.74% and Palakkad at 113.63%. Nagpur and Coimbatore recorded growth of 53.33% and 57.40%, respectively.People aged 26 to 35 accounted for 27.66% of first-time buyers, followed by those aged 36 to 45 at 21.98%. Together, the 26 to 45 age group represented 49.64% of new buyers. Only 7.36% of policies covered families whose eldest member was above 65.Men accounted for 82.81% of first-time buyers, while women made up 17.19%, indicating a substantial gender gap in new health insurance adoption.The average sum insured among first-time buyers doubled from Rs 6.3 lakh in FY22 to Rs 13.1 lakh in FY26. In FY26, 68% of first-time policies offered coverage of Rs 10 lakh or more, compared with 32% in FY22. A Rs 10 lakh cover was the most common choice, accounting for 51% of policies. The data also noted an increase in coverage following the removal of GST in Sept 2025.According to Sarbvir Singh, joint group CEO of PB Fintech, the parent of Policybazaar, growth in health insurance depends on bringing new customers into the system, particularly in smaller cities. "Over the last four years, a growing number of people have taken that step by buying their first health policy, and more of them each year are in Tier 2 and 3 cities. They are in their late twenties and thirties, with families to protect, and they are starting with larger covers than first-time buyers did in FY22," he said.Singh said first-time buyers need help understanding their policies and navigating claims. "Our job is to take them to a policy they understand, and then stand by them at the time of claim," he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: Chennai: Sundram Fasteners Ltd reported a 13% year-on-year increase in consolidated net profit to Rs 172.63 crore for the September quarter, supported by a 30% growth in revenue to Rs 1,984.50 crore.The company’s consolidated revenue for the first half of FY27 rose 25% to Rs 3,830.57 crore, while net profit increased 14% to Rs 341.32 crore from Rs 300.69 crore a year earlier. Profit before tax for the half-year grew 13% to Rs 454.09 crore.The company’s board declared an interim dividend of Rs 4.05 per share, representing 405% of the face value, for FY27. The record date for the dividend is November 6, 2026.On a standalone basis, Q2 revenue rose 32% to Rs 1,760.77 crore, while net profit increased 14% to Rs 159.98 crore. articles.title: KPIT Q2 y-o-y revenue drops 2.2% $176 mn
articles.summary: KPIT Technologies Q2 dollar revenue fell 2.2% YoY to $176.8m; EBIT margin rose to 12.7%. New deal wins totaled $213m amid client declines.
articles.body: Bengaluru: KPIT Technologies reported dollar revenue of $176.8 million for the September quarter, flat sequentially and down 2.2% year on year, as a decline in business from its two largest clients weighed on performance. Revenue from these accounts fell about 13% over the year.In constant currency, revenue grew 0.5% sequentially and 0.2% year on year.EBIT margin improved 40 basis points sequentially to 12.7% from 12.3% in the June quarter. However, it remained below the year-ago level of 16.4%.KPIT also reported a forex loss of Rs 17.1 crore and a share of loss of Rs 15.6 crore from Qorix, both of which management expects to ease from the December quarter. Qorix was founded in 2023 as a joint initiative between KPIT Technologies and the ZF Group to address the growing complexity of automotive software.The company secured new engagements with a total contract value (TCV) of $213 million during the quarter. The wins included a leading American carmaker, two European carmakers, a leading Asian car manufacturer and an American commercial vehicle maker. The projects span powertrain, connected technologies, middleware, autonomous systems, cybersecurity, electric powertrain and aftersales.KPIT ended the quarter with 12,347 employees, an increase of 44 sequentially but a decline of 532 from a year earlier.Geographically, US revenue rose 15.7% sequentially to $62.4 million, while revenue from the SIMA region increased 27.6%. Europe revenue fell 15.2% to $74.5 million.Co-founder and joint managing director Sachin Tikekar said the company was focused on building a more diversified and resilient growth engine. He expects the decline in business from the two large accounts to bottom out over the next couple of quarters.European OEMs continue to face tremendous pressure, with sales continuing to decline and margins under pressure. They are pursuing significant cost-cutting initiatives, and we believe this will continue for a few more quarters. This is primarily due to the competition they face in China, as well as competition from Chinese players in the rest of the world, particularly Europe, Southeast Asia and the Middle East.American OEMs are somewhat protected because a bulk of their revenue comes from the Americas. They continue to be in a relatively better position than their European counterparts. articles.title: Midwest Gasoline Supplies Hit Lowest On Record As Election Nears
articles.summary: Gasoline stockpiles in the Midwest have fallen to an all-time low, raising the threat of persistently high pump prices in the region just days away from a ha...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Gasoline stockpiles in the Midwest have fallen to an all-time low, raising the threat of persistently high pump prices in the region just days away from a handful of crucial Senate elections.

Commercial gasoline supplies declined to 41 million barrels — the lowest on record — after falling by 1.2 million barrels last week, according to US Department of Energy data released Wednesday.

Retail pump prices in the Great Lakes recently soared after a surge in wholesale gasoline blendstock prices in Chicago, the regional benchmark. Production concerns weighed on the benchmark: an issue at a refinery crimped some output, while another facility owned by Cenovus Energy Inc. in Ohio is offline for regular maintenance.

In Michigan, prices averaged $4.69 a gallon on Wednesday, according to GasBuddy, down from highs of around $4.80 a gallon. In Ohio, prices stood around $4.30, also down slightly from last week. Both states have Senate elections next Tuesday that will be critical for deciding the balance of Congress's upper chamber, along with Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska.

Further relief may be on the way in spite of the tight supply picture. Chicago wholesale gasoline blendstock prices have fallen significantly, down to $3.09 a gallon from more than $4 a gallon. Meanwhile, Cenovus's refinery in Ohio appears close to starting back up.

But stockpiles this low mean that any further flare-up might trigger similarly sharp price increases, with little spare fuel on the regional market. And even if no issues emerge, the tight market offers something of a floor to prices.

articles.title: Bank of Canada raises interest rates for the first time in three years
articles.summary: The central bank increased the key rate by a quarter point as soaring energy prices pushed up inflation.
articles.body:
The Bank of Canada (BoC) has raised its key interest rate for the first time in more than three years and warned that further increases might be needed to prevent soaring energy costs from fueling broader inflation.

Wednesday’s quarter-point hike to 2.5 percent was widely expected, while the bank also ramped up its inflation forecast for 2027 to 3.1 percent from the 2 percent it had predicted in July. Growth this year is set to be 1 percent, higher than the 0.7 percent seen in July.

“With the outlook for inflation substantially higher and the economy showing resilience, an increase in the policy rate is needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalised inflation,” BoC governor Tiff Macklem said.

“There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, we will proceed carefully,” he added.

The annual inflation rate hit 3.2 percent in September, above the bank’s 1 to 3 percent target range, and was driven almost solely by higher energy and energy-related transportation costs.

Macklem said inflation was expected to end the year at 3.5 percent and stay at around 3 percent for most of 2027, before returning close to the 2 percent target by the middle of 2028.

“Governing Council agreed that risks to inflation had increased and there was less scope for monetary accommodation,” Macklem said.

The rate hike was the first since July 2023.

“We don’t expect that core measures of inflation will accelerate as much as the bank fears, particularly if global energy prices ease a little, and as a result we don’t think that the policy rate will need to move above 2.75 percent,” said Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Capital Markets.

Money markets are pricing in another 25 basis point rate cut in January and see the benchmark rate going up to 3.25 percent by December next year.

Past experience suggests that businesses will increase the cost of products and services in line with changing costs over the next year, increasing overall inflation, Macklem said.

“The combination of higher energy prices and pass-through increases the persistence of inflation,” he said, although he added that there are lingering uncertainties such as the trade rift with the United States and a faster resolution of the conflict in the Middle East.

Economists who opposed a rise said core inflation, which strips out the cost of volatile items, is still hovering at about 2 percent. They also say a rate hike could impede modest economic recovery, given US trade tensions and a weak job market.

Macklem said new US tariffs would slow the economy in the fourth quarter, but expressed confidence that growth should pick up again in 2027 as consumer spending continues, exports pick up and business investment strengthens.

After a robust annualised growth of 3.3 percent in the second quarter, the economy is likely to slow to 2 percent in the third quarter and further down to 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter, the BoC’s new monetary policy report projected.

The report, however, upgraded its gross domestic product (GDP) forecast for next year and the year after to 2 percent from 1.8 percent for both 2027 and 2028, as predicted in July.

Macklem said this additional growth would help absorb the slack, or its unused capacity, in the economy.

The BoC’s next rate decision is on December 9.

articles.title: Canada-EU summit: What do both sides want, and what’s at stake?
articles.summary: The EU has proposed to make Canada its first associate member amid tensions over US tariffs.
articles.body:
Canada is set to host a summit with the European Union to bolster bilateral strategic and economic ties as its relations with its southern neighbour, the United States, are in sharp decline.

The summit is scheduled for October 29 to 30 in Canada’s French-speaking city of Montreal, and is expected to focus on closer cooperation on trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, research and financial services.

In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the move.

What is the summit, and why is it happening now?

This will be the 21st Canada-EU summit and is expected to build on the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force in 2017. It eliminates duties on up to 99 percent of all imported goods between the two sides, according to the European Council.

“In Montreal, we will take our partnership to the next level by launching our ‘Alliance for the Future’ to deepen our political, economic and institutional ties even further,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, who will be attending the summit along with Carney and von der Leyen. They are expected to issue a joint statement.

The deepening Canada-EU alignment seems fuelled by US President Donald Trump’s policies , which imposed hefty tariffs on both Canadian and European exports to the US and pushed Canada to look for ways to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Before Trump’s tariffs whipsawed relations, Canada sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to the US.

In August, trade talks between Ottawa and Washington, DC, broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

What do Canada and Europe want from each other?

Both sides are seeking opportunities that will open more options beyond the world’s largest economy.

“The opportunity is clear. The EU brings market power, research depth, and manufacturing strength. Canada brings abundant energy, critical minerals, world-class capabilities in space, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum, and one of the world’s strongest banking systems,” Carney’s office said in a statement.

The summit will give the two sides a chance to turn these “complementary strengths into concrete benefits for our peoples,” the statement added.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a think tank in Ottawa, Canada, sees benefits and challenges.

“These fields could be beneficial for both sides, and we are likely to see specific announcements during the summit on these sectors,” she told Al Jazeera.

“The main challenge is how quickly the political momentum can turn into specific deals and projects to deliver specific economic results,” she added.

The EU describes Canada as “the only non-European country” taking part in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s 150 billion-euro ($167bn) loan programme that supports and expedites defence procurement by EU member states.

The EU concluded its agreement with Canada, allowing it to participate under SAFE, in February, and it gives Canadian firms preferential access and treatment in defence procurements financed by the SAFE Instrument.

Could Canada become an associate member of the EU?

Last month, von der Leyen proposed that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, suggesting a deeper relationship spanning trade, technology, defence and economic security.

Carney later welcomed the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.

However, the term “ associate member ” does not currently exist in EU treaties or its standard enlargement framework, according to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels-based think tank.

“The term does not actually matter; what is important is the practical deepening of the relationship and the actual results, no matter what the final term is,” Nadjibulla said.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said in her address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg last month, which Carney attended, making him the first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address.

“I do not see that as an anti-US coalition. It is rather about diversification of economic and defence partnerships and building resilience for Canada. It is a continuation of Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s policies to create opportunities. A deeper alliance with Europe is essential to this agenda,” she said.

“President Trump will likely not appreciate this, but it is about Canada having more choices in an unpredictable world,” she added.

Bob Rae, former premier of Ontario and Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025, told Al Jazeera that “President Trump does not control our policy. We have been having long and productive relations with the Europeans for hundreds of years, but Trump chose to treat Canada in a way that does not respect our sovereignty”.

He added that “engaging in conversations with the EU is perfectly normal and is not directed at the US”.

Trump has threatened the European Union with new tariffs over its proposal to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member”, suggesting the move could be considered hostile to the US.

“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, in September.

Trump dismissed the prospect of Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called the US’s northern neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

articles.title: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.summary: SpaceX stock is back near the $140 floor while smaller space stocks are running ahead.
articles.body:
SpaceX took its worst one-day hit last Thursday since early August, when its biggest share unlock yet freed up to 1.3 billion shares to trade. Roughly a week later, it's back at the same floor, and the rest of the space trade has left it behind.

SpaceX ( SPCX ) shares were sliding again on Wednesday, along with nearly every space stock.

$140 has been SpaceX's floor since the summer. It marked the top of the stock's August trading range before a breakout, and it sits about halfway between the August low near $108 and the $172 ceiling that capped rallies in June and October.

That makes $140 support , a price where buyers have repeatedly stepped in. They did it twice this month, and the stock is back there again.

Smaller space stocks ran past it recently

SpaceX fell about 9% on Oct. 22 as those shares unlocked.

Since then, the smaller names have done the running. Rocket Lab ( RKLB ), Firefly Aerospace ( FLY ), Intuitive Machines ( LUNR ) and AST SpaceMobile ( ASTS ) gained roughly 8% to 14% from the Oct. 22 close through Tuesday, while SpaceX barely budged.

That bounce followed a much rougher month for the group: over the past 30 days, those four are down roughly 20% to 35%, compared with a loss of about 3% for SpaceX.

The pullback comes as investors gear up for Anthropic's IPO, the next mega-listing, with JPMorgan again set to lead retail share sales as it did for SpaceX. SpaceX sits about a third below its June record close near $212.

A sustained break below $140 would open the door to a deeper slide toward the August low near $108. To turn the chart around, bulls first need to get back above the 50-day moving average, near $150, before taking another run at $172.

articles.title: Lionsgate in Investor Talks for Rare Film Library-Backed Bonds
articles.summary: Lionsgate Studios Corp., the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games and other titles, is looking to sell bonds backed by its catalog and talking to investors abou...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Lionsgate Studios Corp., the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games and other titles, is looking to sell bonds backed by its catalog and talking to investors about a possible transaction.

Japanese lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. is arranging early discussions between the film-production company and money managers that may or may not lead to an offering, according to people with knowledge of the matter, asking not to be named as the information is private.

The film studio is in the middle of a turbulent period. Its shares have fallen more than 25% from their peak in June, and activist investor Anson Funds Management is pressing the company to sell itself. Legendary Entertainment has submitted a takeover offer, Bloomberg reported last week, and Anson portfolio manager Sagar Gupta said on Bloomberg TV that Lionsgate could also attract bids from companies including Netflix Inc.

It's not clear how a securitization would fit into Lionsgate's plans. Possible terms of any bonds the company might sell aren't known. A Lionsgate spokesperson declined to comment. MUFG didn't respond to requests for comment.

Companies rarely sell bonds backed by movies and TV shows. The last notable such sale was in 2020, when Village Roadshow Entertainment Group Ltd., owner of movies including the Matrix trilogy, sold $421.5 million of securities.

Lionsgate has more than 20,000 TV shows and movies in its library, including titles such John Wick, according to its website. In May of last year, Lionsgate completed a separation from streaming service and television network Starz Entertainment Corp., which it had acquired in 2016.

Lionsgate had over $1.9 billion of corporate debt as of June 30, according to its latest regulatory filing. That included an intellectual property-linked loan of more than $1 billion due in September 2030, paying 225 basis points over the comparable Secured Overnight Financing Rate, or SOFR. Additionally, every quarter it pays off 2.5% of the total outstanding principal at that time, the filing shows.

The studio's library generates about $1 billion in annual revenue, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Geetha Ranganathan wrote in an Oct. 22 note, adding that Legendary's bid may be the start of the process rather than the end. "I think it could make sense given the deep catalog," she said in an email, when asked about Lionsgate's potential debt offering. "Library-backed bonds could lower funding costs, but the flip side is lower flexibility to use those assets or the catalog in the potential M&A transaction."

articles.title: Precio de la luz por horas mañana jueves 29 de octubre: cuándo es más barata y más cara
articles.standfirst: El precio de la luz se encarece notablemente este jueves
articles.summary: El precio de la luz se encarece notablemente este jueves
articles.body: Hoy, el precio medio de la electricidad se sitúa en 231,01 €/MWh, un aumento de 33,55 € respecto al día anterior, cuando el precio era de 197,46 €/MWh. Este incremento se produce en un jueves, lo que suele ser un día de alta demanda. A medida que avanza la jornada, es crucial observar las horas más caras y más baratas para optimizar el consumo. La luz es más cara durante las horas de mayor demanda, las cuales se concentran principalmente en la tarde y la noche. En particular, las franjas horarias más relevantes son 19:00 - 20:00, 20:00 - 21:00 y 21:00 - 22:00, donde los precios alcanzan picos superiores a 317 €/MWh. Estas horas están intercaladas con tramos costosos durante la tarde, destacando el bloque de 17:00 - 18:00 y 18:00 - 19:00, que también presentan precios elevados, incluso superando los 292 €/MWh. Es evidente que el aumento de la demanda por la tarde y la noche provoca un encarecimiento significativo de la electricidad. El análisis de las franjas horarias revela que la luz es más barata durante la madrugada, ofreciendo importantes oportunidades de ahorro. Las franjas horarias más relevantes para aprovechar precios bajos se concentran entre las 02:00 - 03:00 y 04:00 - 05:00, donde los precios se mantienen por debajo de los 230 €/MWh. Estos periodos son ideales para aquellos que buscan reducir su factura eléctrica, ya que se puede disfrutar de una ventana de precios bajos que abarca varias horas consecutivas, especialmente entre 01:00 - 02:00 y 10:00 - 12:00, donde los valores se encuentran en un rango significativamente más bajo comparado con otros tramos del día. En la jornada de hoy, se presenta una notable diferencia de precios de electricidad, con una diferencia de hasta 183,66 €/MWh entre la hora más cara y la más barata, lo que resalta una significativa volatilidad en las tarifas a lo largo del día. Esta variabilidad puede resultar clave para los consumidores que buscan optimizar sus gastos energéticos.

articles.title: Apple announces $2,899 MacBook Pro — its first touchscreen laptop
articles.summary: Apple has unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook.
articles.body:
Apple ( AAPL ) has done something company observers never thought it would: launched a MacBook with a touchscreen display.

Called the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the laptop gets, you guessed it, an XDR OLED touchscreen, with better colors and brightness than standard LCD displays.

Available in 14-inch and 16-inch options, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also gets the iPhone's Dynamic Island, which houses the laptop's Center Stage webcam. It's also where you'll find Siri AI and Live Activities.

Inside, the notebooks can be outfitted with either Apple's M5 Pro or M5 Max processors.

All of that, however, will cost you: The 14-inch model starts at a wallet-draining $2,899, while the 16-inch will set you back $3,199.

The base MacBook Pro 14-inch with Apple's new M6 processor starts at $1,999. The standard MacBook Pro 16-inch with Apple's M5 Pro processor starts at $2,999.

Those prices represent a $300 increase that Apple implemented in June due to the global memory and storage shortage.

Apple's move to include a touchscreen display with its MacBook comes years after rivals Microsoft ( MSFT ), HP ( HPQ ), Dell ( DELL ), and others implemented the technology in their own laptops.

Apple previously dabbled with touch on its Macs with its Touch Bar, a thin touch-sensitive OLED strip that sat above the keyboard. But the company discarded the feature after it failed to gain traction among users.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display — man, that's a lot of words for a laptop — comes a day after Apple debuted upgraded versions of its MacBook Pro and iMac . The company kicked off the week with a refresh to its iPad mini , which received a larger, improved display and a new processor.

Apple's Mac line of devices accounted for $33.7 billion of the company's $416.1 billion in 2025, making it the tech giant's fourth-largest segment by sales. Apple's iPhone brought in $209.5 billion, while services made up $109.1 billion.

The company has stepped up the cadence of product launches in the second half of the year, bringing out everything from new chips to updated AirPods and more.

The most ambitious device is the iPhone Duo , which is currently sold out in stores, with delivery times extending into late January.

articles.title: Joe Rogan defined the 2024 ‘podcast election.’ But 2026 is a different story
articles.summary: One pithy phrase probably won’t capture all the complexities of the midterm election media environment. Every state is unique, and every race is different. But the tonal shift from 2024 is really striking.
articles.body: If 2024 was a “podcast election,” what’s 2026 shaping up to be? One pithy phrase probably won’t capture all the complexities of the midterm election media environment. Every state is unique, and every race is different. But the tonal shift from 2024 is really striking. This time around, Republicans are not campaigning on “The Joe Rogan Experience” or “This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von.” And the podcasters are not really cheering them on, either. President Trump’s re-election brought story after story about the stupendous influence of Rogan, Von, and other so-called “manosphere” hosts. “The political power of podcasting is only beginning to be felt,” Scott Galloway wrote in a post-election column. The stories weren’t wrong, but those 2024 power players have receded into the background, politically speaking. Rogan has turned into a Trump skeptic, frequently expressing criticism of ICE and the war in Iran. “I can’t believe we went into this war,” Rogan said in April. Moreover, Rogan is not using his show to promote Republican candidates this election cycle. His flattering 2025 interview with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is still circulating, though, and he doesn’t seem like a fan of Talarico’s Republican opponent, Ken Paxton. Other right-leaning podcasters who were outspoken in 2024 are also much more muted this year — reflecting disappointment with Trump and a general malaise about the GOP’s midterm chances. There’s a lot more energy among left-leaning podcasters, though there hasn’t been a single breakout podcast moment this election cycle, a la Trump’s appearance on Rogan’s show in 2024. Dan Pfeiffer, who co-hosts the popular liberal podcast “Pod Save America,” said midterm media strategies are different because the races are different. “Candidates running statewide are going to have different attention strategies than presidential candidates,” Pfeiffer told CNN. Plus, “your target voters in the midterms have different news diets than those in a presidential.” That said, most of the Democratic Senate candidates in battleground states have visited “Pod Save America” this year, some on multiple occasions. Gubernatorial candidates have been frequent guests, too. Some candidates are leaning into the intimate, in-depth format of podcasting more than others. Abdul El-Sayed, for instance, has been on “Pod Save,” “The Weekly Show with Jon Stewart,” and “The Ezra Klein Show” in the past month. El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers, on the other hand, has mostly stuck to local media and national TV. On his podcast, Klein observed that attention and candidate performance seem to be “uncorrelated” right now: “There is almost no connection between who the candidates are who are everywhere, on social media and my feeds, and who are the candidates who are doing particularly well or poorly, at least in polls.” Once the votes are counted, we’ll be much better able to assess which candidates had winning media strategies and which did not. But it seems that podcasts, once a novel and conversational way to reach voters, have been absorbed into the same blob that all media exists in. A candidate sit-down might start as a podcast interview, but by the time someone sees a clip on Instagram, it’s just another piece of talking-head content. Most big podcasts now exist as audio and video; on Apple Podcasts and YouTube. And many other interview formats (like cable news talk shows) now get reformatted as podcasts too. In Iowa, for example, both the Republican Senate candidate, Ashley Hinson, and the Democrat, Josh Turek, made sure to appear on “River to River,” a statewide program that’s both a radio show and a podcast. That’s a very different, and more serious, setting than hangout-style shows like Rogan’s, where guests shoot the breeze for hours on end. In a new story describing Rogan’s “second thoughts” about Trump, Bloomberg’s Ted Mann writes that, in 2024, “Rogan’s benefit to Trump’s political campaign wasn’t just the size of his audience, but the chord he strikes with a cohort of younger, male voters. Those voters, who helped power Trump’s win, are now souring on the administration, if not disengaging altogether.” This is certainly evident in some of the midterm season early-vote data. Political commentator Mark Halperin brought up the absence of a Trump podcast strategy this time around on his “2WAY” show. He called it a mystery: “Why aren’t the president and the vice president on Rogan? Why aren’t they on Andrew Schulz? Maybe because they don’t think the atmosphere would be favorable, as it was two years ago.” It certainly would not be as favorable. Schulz said of Trump, in July 2025, “I voted for none of this. He’s doing the exact opposite of everything I voted for.” And Rogan, in May of this year, called Trump’s IRS settlement and immunity agreement “so crazy” and likened it to something out of a dictatorship: “Then you just go straight Uday Hussein.”

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Cabinet on Wednesday approved the “Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme” (CMPS) with a budgetary outlay of Rs 10,000 crore, aimed at reducing India’s dependence on imports to meet domestic demand and ensuring supply security during crises. China currently accounts for over 95% of global container manufacturing; India aims to expand its container manufacturing to corner a 15% share of the global market.Announcing the decision, I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the scheme will run for 13 years. It was announced in the 2026-27 budget. The move is significant considering that India’s container traffic is projected to grow from around 24 million TEUs in 2024 to 175 million TEUs by 2047.In a post on X, PM Narendra Modi said, “The key benefits of the scheme include 10-fold increase in domestic capacity to 7.5 lakh TEUs annually. Financial support for new and existing manufacturers. Globally competitive, quality-certified containers. Reduced import dependence and stronger supply chains.“ Shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal said the decision “marks a significant step towards building an aatmanirbhar and globally competitive container manufacturing ecosystem in India”.The scheme has three components. First, Interest Subvention Assistance to provide interest subvention of 3% per annum on eligible capital loans for establishment of greenfield container manufacturing facilities and brownfield expansion of existing container manufacturing capacities. Second, Operational Expenditure Assistance with a financial outlay of Rs 8,891 crorewill provide financial assistance for all containers manufactured as per global standards and sold, to bridge cost gap and improve the competitiveness of domestically manufactured containers.In addition, there will be testing and certification assistance to support establishment of common facilities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Apple just announced its first ever MacBook with a touchscreen
articles.summary: Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen. Now it plans to release its first laptop with a touch-sensitive display.
articles.body: Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen. But that all changed on Wednesday when the tech giant announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, its first laptop with a touch-sensitive display. For years, PC makers have been releasing touchscreen computers in an attempt to modernize laptops for the mobile era. Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers. Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO. The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs. Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. The smaller model starts at $2,899, the bigger at $3,399. Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work. It also highlighted its usefulness for graphic designers and musicians, saying they’ll be able to draw sketches and play virtual instruments with just a touch of the screen. The company also claims many existing apps will work with the touchscreen right away because the software will register touches as clicks. The Dynamic Island, or the pill-shaped carveout topping iPhone screens with information and the front camera, will also be included on the new laptop. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also includes additions aimed at creatives, like higher peak brightness than non-touch versions and Adobe’s RGB color space. The company says the touch sensor is built into the display itself rather than layered on top of it, which it claims will reduce latency when swiping and scrolling. Struggles of early touchscreen laptops Touchscreen laptops have existed for more than a decade. Microsoft made a major push to shift the industry in this direction with the release of Windows 8 in 2012. That software featured a new design with larger tile-shaped icons meant to resemble phones and tablets. However, it was widely panned because the operating system was confusing to navigate. The hardware also needed work; early touchscreen laptops were clunky, expensive and awkward to use as tablets. PC makers struggled to keep pace with the rise of smartphones and tablets. “Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event. He said rival laptop makers were trying to “make PCs into tablets and tablets into PCs. Who knows what they will do next?” Despite those early gripes, touchscreen laptops have improved over the years thanks to lower component costs, lighter designs and enhancements to Windows. They’re widely available from major PC makers like Dell and Lenovo. Even Apple, which previously criticized hybrid computers, has been inching in its products in this direction for years. It overhauled the iPad’s software in 2019 with more productivity features, like the ability to use more than one app at once. It’s also made its Mac software look more like the iPhone’s by incorporating elements like the control panel for managing settings and the Liquid Glass translucent design for app icons. Yet touchscreen devices only accounted for 16.3% of global laptop shipments in 2025, according to market research from the International Data Corporation. That’s largely because touchscreens aren’t popular with commercial buyers since most workers just plug their laptop into a monitor when they’re at their desk, according to Ryan Reith, group vice president for the IDC. Apple previously tried incorporating touch technology into the MacBook Pro in 2016 with the introduction of the Touch Bar, a touch-sensitive strip located above the keyboard for accessing app controls and other shortcuts. But it largely flopped with consumers because its utility didn’t justify the additional cost. Apple’s next era Apple is known for being late to technologies – usually for good reason. It wasn’t the first company to launch MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but it made those products popular with consumers by making its devices simpler and easier to use. The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the latest of several recent examples to follow this playbook. The company introduced its HomeView smart home hub earlier this month, attempting to challenge Amazon’s dominance in the smart home industry. And last week, Apple’s first foldable iPhone went on sale, debuting long after chief rival Samsung established a lead in that market. Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise. Wall Street will be watching for signs of how Apple’s new products are being received on the company’s earnings call next week, especially following reports of broken iPhone Duo screens. Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals. “Apple’s entry will not dramatically change the PC market, but it will change the status of touch-enabled laptops,” Francisco Jeronimo, an analyst covering mobile devices and computers, said in an email following Apple’s announcement.

articles.title: Federal Reserve leaves interest rates unchanged despite rising inflation
articles.summary: The soaring costs of gas, diesel and crude oil are a major driver of higher prices across the U.S. economy.
articles.body: The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep interest rates unchanged, its final monetary policy decision before the midterm elections. The decision to hold rates steady came despite inflation that jumped from a 3.4% annual rate in August to 3.7% in September. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also announced that the central bank will reduce the number of meetings at which it votes on interest rates from eight to seven next year and by two in 2028. Warsh said that the seismic change to the schedule would help improve the “quality” of its decisions. A major driver of that inflation is the soaring cost of gas, diesel and crude oil. These higher prices have hit consumers hard, and many economists say the spillover effect of rising gas prices has started to show up across the broader economy. In its post-decision statement, the Fed acknowledged the problem that inflation is causing but said it needs more data before moving forward with a rate hike. “Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal,” it said. The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, will not be released until Thursday; it is expected to touch 3.7%. “This suggests that the Fed might not be done tightening and future hikes will depend on the incoming data,” economists at Morgan Stanley said. In central bank speak, “tightening” refers to raising rates. “As we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction,” Warsh said in a post-meeting news conference. “That’s good news, but inflation is too high.” “Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy,” he added. Wednesday’s vote was not unanimous, unlike September’s 12-0 vote to hike rates, the first time since 2023 that the central bank had raised its benchmark rate. Two officials, governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of a rate hike. The dissent by Cook, whom President Donald Trump is attempting to fire, was her first ever. An interest rate hike could have added slightly more pressure to already beleaguered consumers. Voters have consistently told pollsters that rising prices, especially in the housing and energy sectors, are their primary concerns as they cast their ballots. The most recent NBC News poll found Trump’s approval rating at 27% for his handling of the cost of living and 29% for his handling of the Iran war. Two-thirds of Americans said the soaring gas prices triggered by Trump’s Iran war were either a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. More than half of respondents said current economic conditions had caused them to change what kinds of groceries they buy. Warsh said the midterms and politics “played no role in the decision” to keep rates where they are. Asked about Trump’s recent claims that members of the Fed’s board and rate-setting committee were hostile to the president, Warsh defended his colleagues. “We just came out of a heck of a family fight, serious, sober discussion,” he said. “I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment, and I’m honored to be here and honored to be the chairman of this group.” The central bank also acknowledged the economic anxiety gripping much of the country. “Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” Wednesday’s announcement and the Fed’s acknowledgment that inflation remains well above its goal set the stage for a rate increase during December’s monetary policy meeting.

articles.title: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation
articles.summary: Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation. The central bank’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent. “The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a…
articles.body:
Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation.

The central bank’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent.

“The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters, reiterating the FOMC’s statement.

Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland’s president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Hammack also backed a rate hike in late July, joining two of her colleagues in the minority when the central bank kept rates steady .

Wednesday’s decision came six weeks after officials raised rates by a quarter point , the first hike in more than three years. Inflation has risen this year amid the Iran war , creating a difficult set of circumstances for President Trump and the GOP this midterm cycle .

Warsh said Wednesday he has “started to see some changes” in financial and credit conditions since the Fed raised rates in September.

“They have tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect,” he added. “Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations.”

But the Fed chair noted he was “unwilling and unable” to call financial conditions “tight,” while arguing they are headed “in the direction of achieving a longer or durable period of economic growth and price stability.”

Traders were overwhelming anticipating a hold, pricing in a 92.8 percent chance of the FOMC keeping rates steady as Wednesday afternoon, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Investors expected a hold despite inflation remaining above the Fed’s 2 percent target for five and a half years.

Annual inflation, based on the consumer price index (CPI), rose from 3.4 percent in August to 3.7 percent in September. Energy shocks from the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars continue to hamper the economy, as gas prices in September experienced their highest monthly jump since March.

Multiple Fed officials, though, recently stressed the need to patiently evaluate economic data — a sign they were willing to punt the next rate hike to early December, when the FOMC will meet for the last time in 2026.

Ted Rossman, a finance analyst at Money Management International, said it “seems very likely” the Fed will increase rates by a quarter-point increase in early December.

“Inflation remains uncomfortably high, and the rising cost of living and elevated interest rates are combining to squeeze household budgets,” he told The Hill via email.

Last month, 12 of 18 FOMC officials forecast one more rate hike this year in addition to September’s quarter-point increase, according to the committee’s quarterly economic projections .

“The Fed has time on its side. Inflation expectations remain anchored and second-round effects are limited, giving policymakers room to wait for more data,” Seema Shah, the chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said this week.

Shah added she expects the central bank to hike rates in December and again in “early 2027.”

Warsh did not commit to a future decision on Wednesday, but he said the FOMC is “working on” lowering inflation.

“We will deliver price stability,” the Fed chair said. “No ifs, ands or buts, and that continues to be.”

The Bureau of Economic Analysis on Thursday will release personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index data for September. The Cleveland Fed projects that the PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, will measure prices as being up 3.6 percent from September 2025.

PCE inflation dipped from 3.7 percent in July to 3.4 percent in August . But energy prices experienced their largest monthly jump from August to September, according to the CPI, as the eight-month Iran war continues with no clear end in sight.

Warsh acknowledged the price pressures squeezing Americans, referencing the spike in gas prices during the Middle Eastern conflict .

While a gallon of regular gas is, on average, roughly 23 cents cheaper than it was a month ago, it remains about $1.21 higher than a year ago, according to data from AAA .

“I am not going to be the guy who says that oil prices haven’t gone up, and when [Americans] fill up their tank, they don’t see it,” Warsh said.

Those higher prices pose political problems for Republicans in the midterms , as Democrats attempt to take control of Congress for the lion’s share of Trump’s final two years in office.

Warsh, however, insisted Fed officials did not take politics into account in holding rates steady.

“I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs,” the Fed chair told reporters. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics. I didn’t hear a reference to politics, elections, what’s happening in the next week or so.”

The decision comes six weeks after the Fed raised rates by a quarter point, its first hike in three years, in an effort to rein in stubborn inflation.

Annual inflation climbed to 3.7 percent in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, as price surges tied to President Trump’s war with Iran continue to strain Americans’ wallets.

articles.title: GLP-1s could cause beer sales to take a hit, report says
articles.summary: Options Heineken advised its customers to pursue are half-pints, low- and no-alcohol options, according to the publication.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — One benefit reported by people taking GLP-1 medications is a reduction in alcohol cravings and consumption, but the drugs’ growing popularity has created new challenges for beer companies.

According to Reuters , Heineken presented a document to U.K. hospitality customers earlier this month advising that the medications could potentially change drinking habits among users. The drugs may result in “fullness and fewer serves” in pubs and bars.

“We see some changes in consumption behaviour among (GLP-1) users and will continue to monitor how these behaviours evolve in 2027,” a Heineken spokesperson told the publication.

The report noted that the company’s research found consumers increasingly choosing smaller servings, lower-alcohol beverages and premium products and that these shifts also align with broader trends focused on health, wellness and moderation.

One option Heineken advised customers to pursue is half-pints and low- and no-alcohol options, according to the news wire. Other brewers, including Diageo, Carlsberg and Damm, all had differing opinions on Heineken’s warning.

“It’s really hard for a beer company to do that because of legislative reasons and making sure your claims are right, so I wouldn’t say that we would actively pursue a GLP-1-focused strategy,” Luke White, Damm’s managing director of UK business, told the outlet.

“We’re quite nicely positioned where in our portfolio, in the UK specifically, the two growing areas in the category are no-and-low and world lager,” he continued. “We will be spending a lot more time on the development of the low-and-no sector, be that flavor or new ABV.”

The report also stated that Drinkaware and KAM found that people using GLP-1 medications spent 30 percent less on alcohol when visiting pubs, bars and restaurants, while their weekly spending on alcohol for home consumption fell by 22 percent.

articles.title: Five key takeaways from the UK Autumn Budget
articles.summary: The United Kingdom’s government says its policies are for the ‘working people of Britain’.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom’s government has announced its first budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister and leader of the Labour Party three months ago.

Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey unveiled his Autumn Budget on Wednesday, announcing a series of policies that he said were for the “working people of Britain”, who have experienced a dramatic decline in living standards in recent years. Healey said the budget would give the country “breathing space” after years of economic stagnation fuelled by austerity, Brexit, the coronavirus pandemic, privatisation and rising energy prices.

So, what did Healey announce, and what will it mean for the average Brit?

Global fuel prices have soared in recent months because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has prompted Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway through which about 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) would normally transit.

In response, Healey said on Wednesday that 20 million households will receive a one-off payment of 100 British pounds ($133) towards their energy bills. People living in homes valued at 88,000 British pounds ($117,000) or less will receive the payment. The valuations are based on prices in April 1991, not current house prices.

Healey also said a temporary cut to VAT – a sales tax – will be extended until 1 July. The measure will reduce the annual price cap by 50 British pounds ($66.50).

However, James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the left-wing think tank Verdant, told Al Jazeera that these measures will not tackle the cost-of-living crisis in “any serious way”.

“There’s quite a lot of small things. These are not nothing. They’re just not approaching the scale of the problem that people are already facing and [which] is expected, according to the government’s own figures, to get worse over the next year,” Meadway said.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), an independent public body that analyses the country’s finances, said it expected no growth in real earnings next year. The body also sharply downgraded its growth forecast for 2027 to 1 percent, from 1.5 percent.

“There are forecasts out there saying that by the end of Parliament, it will be the worst Parliament for living standards in modern history. Put in those terms, what you got in this budget was nothing like enough,” Meadway added.

Healey said he would fund the government’s additional Defence Investment Plan, worth 15 billion British pounds ($20bn), and pledged to plug a gap of 4.7 billion British pounds ($6.2bn) by “reprioritising” budgets across other departments.

However, he did not detail how the government would meet its NATO commitment to spend 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2035, with an interim target of three percent in 2030. Instead, Healey said he would set out how these targets would be met during a spending review next year.

In response, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte welcomed the British government’s budget plan, saying it showed a “strong commitment” ⁠to defence.

“Good news on the new budget from MP John Healey with ‌a strong commitment on defence,” wrote Rutte on X.

“The UK role in Transatlantic security is vital, and I welcome ⁠this move to ⁠put Britain on a credible path towards meeting the commitment ⁠made by all NATO Allies ⁠in The Hague – ⁠to ensure we’re all investing what’s needed to remain ready ‌and able to deter aggression and defend our freedom ‌and ‌security,” Rutte added.

Ukraine was also on the agenda during Healey’s budget statement, with the chancellor pledging an additional 10 billion British pounds ($13.2bn) in economic and military aid for Kyiv in its war with Russia.

The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage will both increase by 3.9 percent in April, at the start of the new tax year. The former currently sets a minimum hourly rate of 10.85 British pounds ($14.44) for workers aged 18 to 20, while the latter sets the rate at 12.71 British pounds ($16.91) for workers aged 21 and over.

To raise funds for additional support for households and businesses, the government will temporarily increase the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from three percent to six percent. The increase will last for 15 months, ending on March 31, 2028. The surcharge is levied on top of standard corporation tax and is expected to raise 1.5 billion British pounds ($2bn).

Affordable housing is a significant problem in the UK. The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) shows that 35 percent of men aged 20 to 35 were living at home with their parents last year, compared with 22 percent of women in the same age range.

To tackle this, Healey announced a new First Time Buyer savings account. Interest earned in such accounts, commonly referred to as Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs), is tax-free.

The First Time Buyer account will launch in 2029, replacing the current Lifetime ISA. The exact details of the new account are not yet clear. However, like the Lifetime ISA, it will pay savers a bonus of 25 percent on deposits of up to 4,000 British pounds ($5,320). That means savers can benefit from an annual government bonus of up to 1,000 British pounds ($1,330).

Healey also announced that the penalty for first-time buyers using funds from a Lifetime ISA to purchase a house worth more than 450,000 British pounds ($598,853) will immediately be reduced to 20 percent. That means savers will get back at least what they put in. The penalty was previously 25 percent.

A further 432 million British pounds ($574.9m) will also be spent over the next two years to reduce the number of people sleeping on the streets, a problem that Burnham has pledged to end.

articles.title: KPIT Q2 YoY revenue drops 2.2% $176 million
articles.summary: KPIT Q2 revenue fell 2.2% YoY to $176.8m as top clients declined; EBIT margin rose to 12.7%. New deals totaled $213m amid OEM pressures.
articles.body: Bengaluru: KPIT Technologies reported dollar revenue of $176.8 million in the September quarter, flat sequentially and down 2.2% year on year, as a decline in business from its two largest clients weighed on performance. Revenue from these accounts fell about 13% over the year.In constant currency, revenue grew 0.5% sequentially and 0.2% year on year.EBIT margin improved 40 basis points sequentially to 12.7% from 12.3% in the June quarter. However, it remained below the year-earlier level of 16.4%.KPIT also reported a forex loss of Rs 17.1 crore and a share of loss of Rs 15.6 crore from Qorix. Management expects both to ease from the December quarter. Qorix was founded in 2023 as a joint initiative between KPIT Technologies and the ZF Group to address the growing complexity of automotive software.The company secured new engagements with a total contract value (TCV) of $213 million during the quarter. The wins included a leading American carmaker, two European carmakers, a leading Asian carmaker and an American commercial vehicle maker. The projects span powertrain, connected technologies, middleware, autonomous systems, cybersecurity, electric powertrain and aftersales.KPIT ended the quarter with 12,347 employees, an increase of 44 sequentially but a decline of 532 from a year earlier.Geographically, US revenue rose 15.7% sequentially to $62.4 million, while revenue from the SIMA region increased 27.6%. Europe revenue fell 15.2% to $74.5 million.Co-founder and joint managing director Sachin Tikekar said the company was focused on building a more diversified and resilient growth engine. He expects the decline in business from its two largest accounts to bottom out over the next couple of quarters.European original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) continue to face significant pressure, with sales declining and margins under strain. They are pursuing substantial cost-cutting initiatives, which are expected to continue for a few more quarters. This is primarily due to competition in China and from Chinese players in other markets, particularly Europe, Southeast Asia and the Middle East.American OEMs are relatively protected because a bulk of their revenue comes from the Americas. articles.title: Fed plans to eliminate some rate-setting meetings, chairman says
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve plans to eliminate some meetings devoted to setting interest rates in the next couple of years, Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.
articles.body: The Federal Reserve plans to eliminate some meetings devoted to setting interest rates in the next couple of years, Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday. Starting next fall, the central bank will dedicate one of its eight annual meetings to considering broad-based questions about the economy, rather than to voting on interest rates, Warsh said. That number will increase to two in 2028. The chairman made the announcement following the release of the central bank’s latest policy announcement, which left rates unchanged. He said the rationale for doing so was to devote more time to thinking about longer-term issues by shifting attention away from the immediate interest rate environment. “Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information-rich intervals,” he said. “But it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.” Warsh’s announcement marks a major shake-up for the Federal Reserve’s long-standing policy calendar, which is closely watched by investors around the world. The Federal Open Market Committee has held eight scheduled meetings a year since 1981. Warsh began seriously discussing a reduction in rate-setting meetings in July, according to the FOMC’s meeting minutes, arguing that a longer lag between rate-setting meetings would allow the committee to accumulate more data about the economy. Reducing the number of rate-setting meetings has long been debated over concerns about shortsightedness — but the switch was never enacted over fears that the Fed would become less nimble in reacting to sudden changes in the economy. The change would make the Fed unique among major central banks, including the Bank of England and Bank of Japan. It marks another major change enacted by Warsh, who took the reins of the Fed in May after being nominated by President Donald Trump. Warsh has dramatically shortened the FOMC’s post-meeting policy statement. He has also declined to issue what is known as “forward guidance,” which contains forecasts about future inflation and unemployment.

articles.title: Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US
articles.summary: Rates will remain 3.75-4 percent even as inflation continues to rise.
articles.body:
The United States Federal Reserve is set to hold interest rates steady in its final monetary policy decision before the US midterm elections.

The central bank will maintain rates at 3.75-4 percent, following a 10-2 vote, in line with expectations.

CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, indicated that there was more than a 90 percent chance rates would remain unchanged.

“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the Fed said in its press release announcing the decision on Wednesday. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”

The Fed noted how inflation continues to rise.

It also added, “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”

The most recent Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed the annual inflation rate increasing to 3.7 percent in September , up from 3.4 percent in August, with energy prices largely accounting for the monthly surge.

There were signs earlier this month that the central bank would maintain benchmark interest rates, with the Fed’s chair for supervision, Michelle Bowman, advocating a “wait and see” approach.

“I don’t feel any urgency for taking further action at this point,” she said at this month’s International Monetary Fund-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. “We really need to take some time and understand how things will evolve.”

The decision comes before Thursday’s release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index report, which is used by the central bank to assess inflation and inform its decisions.

Today’s Fed announcement follows an interest-rate hike rise last month, amid surging inflation – the first increase by the central bank since July 2023. The move drew criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed the Fed to cut rates since taking office. At the time, he wrote on Truth Social that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”

The Fed’s next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9, when it will give its final rate decision of the year.

Current forecasts point to a quarter-point interest rate increase.

articles.title: US Federal Reserve keeps rates unchanged, leaves door open to further hikes
articles.summary: The US Federal Reserve held interest rates unchanged at 3.75%-4% in a 10-2 vote, as policymakers weighed persistent inflation against a resilient economy
articles.body: The US Federal Reserve held interest rates unchanged at 3.75%-4% in a 10-2 vote, as policymakers weighed persistent inflation against a resilient economy and waited for further data before deciding their next move. The decision came ahead of next week’s US midterm elections, with the central bank acknowledging that inflation remains elevated despite signs of continued economic strength.Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said economic activity was expanding at a “strong” pace, upgrading the Fed’s assessment from “solid” at its September meeting. Domestic spending remained resilient, productivity growth was strong, investment robust and job gains had kept pace with the workforce, while the unemployment rate had changed little. However, inflation continues to run above the Fed’s 2% target, leaving policymakers divided over whether monetary policy needs to tighten further.Governors Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented from the decision, favouring a 25-basis-point rate hike. Their position reflects concerns that inflationary pressures remain persistent and that delaying further tightening could make it harder to bring price increases under control. Some economists and market participants have also suggested that another rate hike could come in December, although the Fed has not committed to a specific course.Warsh said the central bank needed more information to determine the appropriate policy stance, stressing that tackling inflation could not be tied to a fixed date or a single data point. He added that inflation expectations had moved in the right direction since the Fed’s September policy action, while financial and credit conditions had tightened for some businesses and households. However, he said he was unwilling to describe overall financial conditions as tight.Markets reacted cautiously to the decision. US stock indexes were mixed, Treasury yields edged higher and short-term interest rate futures rose, reflecting uncertainty over the path of monetary policy.
