articles.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico expand lawsuit against Trump White House, citing continued ‘viewpoint discrimination’
articles.summary: CNN, MS NOW and Politico have amended their lawsuit against President Donald Trump’s White House press ban, citing “continued retaliatory and viewpoint-discriminatory deprivation” by the Trump administration.
articles.body: CNN, MS NOW and Politico have amended their lawsuit against President Donald Trump’s White House press ban, citing “continued retaliatory and viewpoint-discriminatory deprivation” by the Trump administration. The three news outlets are once again accusing the administration of violating the First and Fifth Amendments. The updates to the lawsuit concern the White House’s interference with the press pool, a decades-old tradition that has news outlets take turns covering the president in close quarters, including Air Force One and the Oval Office. In recent weeks, the Trump administration has repeatedly excluded CNN and Politico from Trump’s Air Force One trips, even after a federal judge issued an order halting Trump’s broader original ban. “To be clear,” the expanded lawsuit states, the news outlets “do not claim an unrestricted right to enter the Oval Office or travel aboard Air Force One. But once the White House opens those spaces to selected journalists for newsgathering and reporting, the White House may not exclude plaintiffs because it dislikes their coverage.” Last week, the outside counsel for the three news outlets, Ted Boutrous, threatened further legal action if the White House continued to bar reporters from specific areas, such as Air Force One. Boutrous asked for confirmation that the administration would “abandon any policy of excluding CNN from the Oval Office and Air Force One” and stop preventing assigned pool reporters from doing their duties. The administration did not respond. So Wednesday afternoon’s court filing is the next step. The amended complaint asks the court for another ruling in favor of the news outlets: “The court should declare unlawful the President’s ban of plaintiffs and the White House’s further unconstitutional actions, including its continued exclusions of plaintiffs from specific White House press areas for retaliatory and viewpoint-discriminatory reasons, and enter permanent injunctive relief in favor of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico.” The amended complaint comes two weeks after US District Judge Timothy P. Kelly granted a preliminary injunction restoring the outlets’ White House access, finding that Trump’s ban likely violated the First Amendment by discriminating against journalists based on their coverage of his administration. Kelly had previously issued a temporary restraining order on Fifth Amendment grounds. The administration is appealing Kelly’s ruling. When a CNN reporter asked the White House for comment about the amended lawsuit on Wednesday, a White House official said, “the Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office.” The White House complied with Kelly’s court’s order and reinstated journalists’ press credentials late last month, but CNN, MS NOW and Politico say the administration has continued to retaliate against them by disrupting the press pool. CNN has been barred from traveling aboard Air Force One on all six occasions when it was scheduled to serve as the designated TV network pooler since Trump announced the ban on September 18. The TV pool role is one that “CNN has fulfilled for more than four decades,” the revised lawsuit points out. The five major US TV networks have a well-established pool rotation, and the other networks have shown support for CNN amid the dispute. Politico has also been barred twice from its scheduled out-of-town pool assignments in recent weeks. And MS NOW “has not participated in the secondary television pool since September 18,” the day Trump announced the ban, the revised lawsuit states. The secondary pool spot is selected by the White House. When blocking the news outlets from fulfilling pool duties, the administration appears to be relying on an ongoing court case involving The Associated Press, which filed suit last year when Trump blocked AP reporters from areas with limited space for the press pool. Trump took action against The AP because the news wire didn’t immediately start using his new name for the Gulf of Mexico like he wanted. In June 2025, an appeals court panel partially lifted the stay obtained by The AP and stated that the news wire was not likely to succeed on the merits “because these restricted presidential spaces” like Air Force One and the Oval Office “are not First Amendment fora opened for private speech and discussion.” But the ruling was “non-binding and non-precedential,” as Boutrous pointed out in his letter last week, so it is not binding on other cases. The revised lawsuit asserts that the Oval Office and Air Force One have been “two of the primary spaces for journalists to interact with, gather news about, and publish reporting on President Trump and other officials.” “While the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room remains a critical forum for reporters to gather and report the news, of the nearly 5,000 questions the President has entertained from reporters in these traditional areas, 97% were either in the Oval Office or in connection with his travel aboard Air Force One,” the lawsuit states. Boutrous said in a statement on Wednesday that by excluding the banned news outlets from spaces like Air Force One, the administration is continuing “to violate the First Amendment and due process.” “These exclusions, intended to punish and chill coverage of the administration that the President doesn’t like, make it harder for the press to cover some of the most important events in the world for the benefit of the American people,” Boutrous said. “CNN, MS NOW and Politico will continue to fight to vindicate their rights to report the news.”

articles.title: Did the Fed just make a huge mistake?
articles.summary: The cost of living is Issue No. 1 for voters heading to the polls, but the Federal Reserve saw America’s persistent inflation problem Wednesday and opted not to do anything about it.
articles.body: The cost of living is Issue No. 1 for voters heading to the polls, but the Federal Reserve saw America’s persistent inflation problem Wednesday and opted not to do anything about it. At least for the next six weeks, anyway. Despite consumer prices gaining 3.7% over the past year and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge stubbornly remaining 50% above the central bank’s target, the decision to hold interest rates steady was widely expected. That’s because changing rates is a blunt instrument that can inflict serious damage on the economy when ill-timed or used improperly. “Interest rates get in the cracks,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a press briefing Wednesday. “They affect everything.” Central bankers just last month hiked rates for the first time in more than three years, and they want to wait a bit to see how the economy responds before bashing it over the head again with another rate hike. “Ensuring price stability and watching inflation is not about some fixed date on a calendar or some isolated data point,” Warsh said. “It’s about ensuring we have clear objectives and the right monetary policy.” Warsh said he was encouraged by the reduction in inflation expectations since the Fed raised rates in September. By waiting, however, the Fed is also taking a significant gamble. The Fed risks another 2021-like mistake, when it assumed the inflation monster staring the economy directly in the face could be defeated by just ignoring it. (The Fed was disastrously wrong). This time may truly be different, and not acting with haste could prove prescient. Or it could force the central bank to give the economy some December shock therapy that it may have been able to avoid with an October rate hike. Why the Fed didn’t hike Jobs. Hiking rates increases businesses’ borrowing costs, which leaves them with less money to hire. Now may be a perilous time to mess with the job market: The US economy added only 29,000 jobs in September, well below expectations. And the September report showed that the economy added 60,000 fewer jobs over the previous two months than previously believed. The labor market is by no means in bad shape, but it has been on shaky ground. The US economy lost 10,000 jobs in July and in seven of the past 16 months. Although unemployment remains at a healthy 4.2%, economists describe the economy as “low hire, low fire.” In other words, your position may not be at risk, but if you leave your job, you may have trouble finding a new one. Markets. Treasury yields moved higher since the last Fed rate hike, with bond yields at one point hitting multi-decade highs. Yields have slipped a bit since, returning to where they were in mid-September, but the still relatively high bond yields can help give the Fed cover, because they have an effect similar to the Fed funds rate, slowing the economy and inflation. The Fed also doesn’t like to surprise investors – even in Warsh’s new keep-‘em-guessing era. The market had priced in a 91% chance that the Fed would hold rates, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, and a hike could have sent the markets into a painful rebalancing. Timing. The Fed’s decision may also have been influenced, at least somewhat, by the upcoming election. Narayana Kocherlakota, the former Minneapolis Fed president, told my colleague Matt Egan that the Fed hesitated to raise rates Wednesday because it wanted insulation from President Donald Trump’s criticism. But the Fed throughout its history has changed rates many times just as voters were heading to the polls, my colleague Elisabeth Buchwald also noted. Why holding could be a mistake The “transitory” error: The Fed typically doesn’t get involved when supply shocks like the Iran-war-induced energy crisis cause inflation. They’re notoriously temporary, hard to predict and insensitive to rate changes. But supply shocks sometimes lead to bigger problems that the Fed can help fix. The Fed should know: It just went through this. As the economy emerged from the pandemic, the Fed made a mistake with inflation, declaring it a result of a “transitory” supply shock related to the Russia-Ukraine war and massive supply chain snarls. It ended up becoming the most significant inflation problem in a generation. The Fed, caught off guard, was forced to raise rates at a historic pace – three consecutive hikes of three-quarters of a percentage point. Ultimately, the Fed succeeded at lowering out-of-control inflation to more manageable levels, but not before consumer prices peaked at an annual rate of 9.1%, the highest in four decades. This time may be no different: Inflation is already spilling over into other parts of the economy. Particularly concerning in the September consumer inflation report was the surprising rebound in housing and rent costs, a significant contributor to inflation that had cooled off in the spring and summer. And the cost of other services rose higher than expected, too – prices that tend to rise (and stay high) as yoga studios, lawn services and the like charge their customers more to make up for their rising costs. Also driving inflation: Investment in data centers and technology powering AI has propelled the economy into overdrive – and maybe helped overheat it. Prices for electricity, building materials, labor, and personal tech like smartphones and laptops have all risen as a result. More war? This energy price spike could get worse before it gets better. Trump has strongly hinted (and CNN has reported) that the United States and Israel could escalate the war with Iran after the midterm elections, potentially sending oil prices higher. It would be foolhardy for the Fed to make a decision based on a rumor. And energy prices can quickly swing lower. For example, the Trump administration’s announcement of an energy ceasefire in Russia has held surprisingly well, dramatically increasing the amount of diesel Russia produced in the past couple weeks, which could significantly lower global diesel prices – if Ukraine continues to hold off on its drone strikes on Russian refineries. But the prolonged energy price spike is already raising prices across the economy, and waiting to hike again could place the Fed behind the curve. Boiling frogs. Rate hikes work with a delayed effect, and sharper rate changes can have deleterious effects on the financial system, markets and the economy. This economic frog tends to stay in the pot when the heat is turned up gradually. If escalations in the Iran war and Russia-Ukraine war resume, that could force the Fed into a difficult position of hiking rates by even more than expected in its next meeting in December – potentially by a half point, in a kind of make-up call. The massive, successive rate hikes throughout 2022 sent the stock market into its biggest annual decline since the financial crisis and put the housing market on ice. But the economy didn’t go into a recession – a trick the Fed has rarely pulled off when it hikes rates. It’s not a wager a lot of economists are eager to place again.

articles.title: T-Mobile Boosts Profit, Accounts as Network and Offers Resonate
articles.summary: T-Mobile US Inc. added more total customer accounts in the third quarter than analysts had expected, showing its slate of offers and loyalty incentives are r...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- T-Mobile US Inc. added more total customer accounts in the third quarter than analysts had expected, showing its slate of offers and loyalty incentives are resonating with customers.

The Bellevue, Washington-based carrier added 274,000 net monthly accounts, which include mobile phone and broadband internet, in the period, the company said in a statement on Wednesday. That compared with the 251,000 Wall Street was expecting, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. It's also seeing more revenue per account, with an average of $155.73 in the quarter, up 4% from a year earlier.

That helped boost profit 27% from a year ago to $3.5 billion. Earnings per share of $3.22 beat estimates of $2.93, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

T-Mobile and its main two telecom rivals have been under pressure as the market factors in a potential new competitor in Elon Musk's SpaceX, which is emerging as a potential fourth national wireless carrier. To stay competitive, T-Mobile rolled out new plans on Monday that allow customers to pick and choose benefits like streaming, food delivery and device promotions. It has also found success in fostering customer loyalty with its T-Mobile Tuesdays program, which offers customers weekly freebies.

Musk's efforts will require billions of dollars in investment and take years before a new wireless phone carrier is up and running. But the Big Three are already positioning themselves to try to stay ahead. T-Mobile has an existing partnership with SpaceX's Starlink internet service that gives customers access to satellite coverage that can fill gaps in T-Mobile's ground-based network, especially in extremely remote areas.

T-Mobile Chief Technology Officer John Saw recently tried to temper any enthusiasm for Musk's ambition by explaining that SpaceX's recent purchase of 800 MHz spectrum is far from the "last critical piece" needed to create a viable network. "There's a big difference between owning spectrum and delivering a great mobile experience to millions of customers," Saw wrote in a recent post on LinkedIn.

T-Mobile no longer discloses changes in wireless customer additions as a separate metric. But it said service revenue, which include mobile phone plans and on-premises internet, increased 9% from a year ago $16.3 billion, a touch ahead of estimates.

articles.title: Ford reports Q3 earnings beat, tightens lower end of profit forecast but sees $4 billion in EV losses for year
articles.summary: Ford reported third quarter earnings that topped estimates, and upped the lower end of its profit guidance. The company still sees EV losses piling up by the...
articles.body:
Ford ( F ) reported third quarter earnings that topped estimates and upped the lower end of its profit guidance. The company still sees EV losses piling up by the end of the year.

For the quarter, Ford reported automotive revenue of $46.1 billion vs. $46.2 billion, per Bloomberg consensus, with adjusted EPS of $0.49 vs. $0.41, and adjusted EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) of $2.66 billion vs. $2.38 billion.

Ford tightened the low end of its full-year adjusted EBIT guidance to between $10.5 billion and $11 billion (from $10 billion to $11 billion seen prior); analysts projected full-year adjusted EBIT of $10.52 billion. Ford's adjusted free cash flow guidance remained at $6 billion to $7 billion.

Ford sees commodity headwinds approaching $2.5 billion year over year (up from $2 billion last quarter) and US industry pricing "about 100 basis points" higher year over year.

On the flip side, Ford sees $1 billion in material and warranty cost reductions, excluding tariffs and the costs of the Novelis factory fire. Ford CFO Sherry House said on a call with reporters that Ford is seeing some increases in steel and copper prices, and expects more price inflation in 2027.

"We are still expecting significant commodity cost increases going into 2027, accompanied by logistics cost increases due to fuel costs rising and also chip prices increasing moderately this year, but more significantly next year and beyond," House said.

Despite this, House added that she sees Ford's full-year 2027 profit "roughly in line" with 2026 results.

Ford's Model e EV business unit posted a Q3 loss of $1.06 billion vs. an estimated $1.17 billion on revenue of $1.2 billion vs. $1.12 billion, down 31% from a year ago, when the federal EV tax expired at quarter-end. In July, Ford said its Model e outlook included about $1 billion in added spending on its Universal EV platform and Ford Energy, mostly in the second half. Ford projects Model e will lose another $4 billion in 2026.

Last week, rival GM narrowed its 2026 EBIT-adjusted guidance to $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion while raising its EPS outlook; shares slid despite an earnings beat, with investors hoping for more.

One area that may have negatively impacted operations occurred at the end of the quarter in September. Ford canceled all production crews at its Dearborn Truck Plant for nearly a week because of a supply problem, according to Reuters , and Kansas City Assembly cut shifts too.

Ford called it "a short-term supplier issue unrelated to aluminum" and said the hit is "containable within the full-year 2026 adjusted EBIT guidance."

articles.title: Oracle stock soars as it promises the AI spending will start paying for itself
articles.summary: Oracle laid out how its AI build-out turns into cash, and the stock had its best day since April.
articles.body:
For months, investors have asked how Oracle ( ORCL ) would pay for its AI build-out. On Wednesday the company put numbers on it, and the stock had its best day since May.

Shares closed up about 11% at about $144 Wednesday, adding more than $40 billion in market value, as the company laid out new financial targets at its investor day. Even with the jump, the stock is still down about 25% this year.

The stock barely moved for most of the session, hovering near $130 until about 2:20 p.m. ET. Within minutes, it was up 13% after Oracle's release crossed.

Oracle said it expects about $30 billion in free cash flow , the cash left over after paying for data centers and other spending, in its fiscal year ending May 2029. It burned through about $24 billion in the fiscal year that ended this May. The company also said it would limit new fundraising, a mix of stock and debt, to $20 billion through May 2030, and that capital spending would start falling in fiscal 2029 after peaking.

Oracle stuck with its goal of $225 billion in revenue in fiscal 2030. It also reaffirmed its outlook for the current fiscal year, including at least $90 billion in revenue.

Investors this year have worried about how much debt Oracle and other AI cloud providers are taking on to build data centers, and the fundraising cap speaks directly to that. Before the investor day, Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer pointed out on X that credit worries were back, citing the rising cost of insuring Oracle and CoreWeave ( CRWV ) debt against default.

"The bond market is regulating as it always does," wrote Timmer, Fidelity's director of global macro. He added that "a more disciplined allocation of capital today will prevent a bursting bubble tomorrow."

Wednesday's gain was one of Oracle's biggest since September 2025. That month, the stock soared 36% in a single day, its best since 1992, after the company reported a surge in contracted AI cloud business. Shares then lost more than half their value from that record as investors questioned how Oracle would fund the build-out, bottoming near $115 in July.

The rally spread to the companies that supply and run AI data centers. Vertiv ( VRT ), which makes power and cooling equipment, jumped about 16%. Memory makers SK Hynix ( SKHY ) and Sandisk ( SNDK ) rose 8% to 13%, and Micron ( MU ) gained about 6%. CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ), which rent out AI computing power, each rose about 7%. Bloom Energy ( BE ) and Quanta Services ( PWR ) gained around 5%.

The biggest AI names didn't join in. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Meta ( META ) each fell about 1%, and Microsoft ( MSFT ) ended flat.

articles.body: US stocks edged higher on Wednesday as investors digested the Federal Reserve's 10-2 decision to hold interest rates steady and focus shifted to earnings results from Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOG). The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) gained roughly 0.2% and 0.3%, respectively. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) climbed roughly 0.3%Investor attention turned toward the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, where the Fed voted to keep its funds rate unchanged, despite elevated inflation readings. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Fed Governor Lisa Cook dissented, favoring a rate hike. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also announced the central bank will have one less policy-setting meeting next year.Sentiment in the tech trade has markedly improved this week, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq posting back-to-back gains. Semiconductor stocks rose for a third day in a row after South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix (SKHY, 000660.KS) reported a 632% year-over-year profit increase. Peeres Micron (MU) and Samsung (005930.KS), also gained. Oracle (ORCL) shares jumped after the software and cloud computing giant issued a fiscal 2030 revenue outlook of $225 billion, implying 35% annual growth.Earnings season continues apace as two Big Tech giants and cloud leaders — Microsoft and Alphabet — deliver updates on AI demand and their capex plans after the bell. Microsoft's report comes just after it offered buyouts to up to 60,000 employees as it tries to streamline operations amid the AI build-out.

articles.title: Indian gaming studios face challenges in monetisation with just $2 revenue per user: Report
articles.summary: GDAI report: India’s 511M gamers generate just $2.04 ARPU; 74% of studios earn under 10% revenue domestically, citing low willingness to pay.
articles.body: Chennai: Despite a massive user base of 511 million players, the Indian market struggles to monetise, according to a report by the industry body Game Developer Association of India (GDAI). India’s gaming revenue is estimated at $1.04 billion in 2025, growing 14.8% year-on-year, but has an annual revenue per user of just $2.04, it said. The industry faces challenges in converting audience scale into commercial value and Indian studios continue to rely heavily on international partnerships for financing, market knowledge, and distribution.Based on a survey, the GameDev Outlook 2026 report said 74% of responses indicate that less than 10% of studio revenue comes from India.It cites low willingness to pay as the second-biggest barrier to market growth, beyond capital and publishing investment. The GDAI report identifies access to capital, publishing expertise, production capabilities, and market access as critical enablers for studios seeking to turn creative ideas into commercially viable games. “Access to overseas players, publishers, investors and clients is therefore not a secondary consideration but is central to commercial viability for a larger share of development stage. Strengthening go-to-market (GTM) capability and making easier, more structured access to publishers and investors is therefore one of the highest priorities for the ecosystem,” it said.The report was released at the India Game Developer Conference (IGDC) in Chennai on Wednesday. It highlights the opportunity for Indian developers to move beyond domestic audience growth and build original intellectual property (IP) with international appeal. It also noted that female participation is approaching half of the player base and non-battle royale titles are gaining share in mobile revenue.
